text: Open Page: what's the one line in your proposals that wins you the most work? Share it. Someone just starting out needs it.
Somewhere right now a designer is kerning a pricing table at midnight. We see you. Go to bed. The client reads it at 9.
The right-hand page of a book is called the recto. It's where the eye lands first, so it's where printers put what matters. That's the whole idea behind the name.
Before you hit send: five things every proposal needs, in this order.

1. Their problem, in their words. Proof you listened.
2. What you'll do. Scope, not adjectives.
3. When. A timeline with real dates.

4. What it costs and how it's paid. Deposit, milestones, done.
5. What happens next. One clear step.
Everything else is decoration. Make the decoration good, but never let it replace these five.
Pricing tables in Recto multiply and total themselves as you type. Change a quantity at 1am, the total is still right at 9am.
The real creative brief is the second email. The first one is what they think they want.
Kurdish has letters many Arabic-script fonts were never drawn for: ڕ ڵ ێ ۆ ە. If a font can't set them, it isn't ready for Kurdish, however beautiful it looks.
A good case study answers one question: why should I trust you with mine?
White space isn't empty. It's the part of the page that tells the reader where to look.
Friday-afternoon proposals get read on Monday morning, under forty other emails. Send it when they have time to read it.
Your logos, colours and fonts, saved once in a brand kit. Apply them to a whole document in one click. Every template in Recto starts from your brand, not ours.
Freelancing is 40% design, 30% email, 20% chasing invoices and 10% wondering if you should have been an accountant.
Open Page: designers, writers, presenters. What's the strangest piece of client feedback you've ever had? Keep it anonymous. Keep it kind. Keep it funny.
Writers make good clients for designers. They already know every word on the page has to earn its place.
A deck has one job per slide. If a slide has two jobs, it's two slides.
Stop sending PDFs into the void. A link tells you if they opened it, how long they stayed on the pricing page and where they stopped reading. That's not surveillance. That's knowing when to call.
A Recto link opens three ways: as a magazine spread, a page-turning book or plain slides. Same document. You choose how your client meets it.
The deposit is not rude. The deposit is the client saying yes with their money, not just their mouth.
Designing in two scripts on one page is a skill few design schools teach. English left to right, Kurdish right to left, both looking like they belong there. It's hard. It's worth it.
Presenters: your slides are not your notes. If you can read your talk off the screen, so can the audience, and they'll do it faster than you.
Good type goes unnoticed. Bad type is the only thing anyone remembers.
A rate card is a confidence document. If you hesitate on the number in person, put it on a page that doesn't.
Clients can pin a comment to the exact spot on your page. No account, no login, no "which slide did you mean". Just a note where the problem is.
Studio rule: don't present three options when you believe in one. Three options is how you ask the client to do your job.
Open Page: which studio, designer or writer in your city deserves more attention? Tag them. Let's give the stage away.
The best portfolios don't show everything. They show what you want to be hired for next.
Page numbers are a kindness. "See page 7" is a conversation. "See the slide with the blue chart" is an argument.
Before you hit send: how to write a scope your client can't misread.
Write what's in. Then write what's out. The second list prevents more arguments than any contract.
Number the rounds of revisions. "Revisions included" means unlimited to the person paying.
Put a date on everything. "Soon" is not a deadline.
Paste straight from Illustrator onto a Recto page. No exporting, no screenshots of your own work.
The client who says "make it pop" isn't wrong. They're telling you it doesn't move them yet. Your job is to find out why, not to add a gradient.
For years, designers here were told good work should look like it came from somewhere else. We think the most interesting brands of the next decade will look like where they're from.
A case study that works: the problem, the decision, the result. Most people skip the decision. The decision is the only part that's yours.
A4 is a desk. 16:9 is a screen. Square is a feed. Know where your document will be read before you design the first page.
Before and after is the most persuasive layout in design. Put the old next to the new, add one number, stop talking.
Case study blocks in Recto come with before/after, metrics and testimonials already laid out. You bring the work. The page already knows how to show it.
Nobody went to design school to learn how to write an invoice. And yet, here we all are.
Open Page, weekend edition: show us a document you're proud of sending. Not the work itself. The proposal, the deck or the case study that won it.
Your proposal will be forwarded to someone you've never met. Design it for them too.
Hierarchy is just the answer to one question: what should they read first, what second, and what must they never skip?
Most pitch decks open with the logo, then "about us", then the team. Three slides about you before one about them. Start with them.
Recto comes with more than 60 commercial fonts, Arabic and Kurdish faces included, ready for client work. One less licence to worry about.
Small studios don't compete on size. They compete on attention. A client can always tell when someone actually read their brief.
English and Kurdish on the same page, each in its own direction, neither one broken. In Recto any text box can run right-to-left. A small switch that saves a whole afternoon.
A proposal that's easy to say yes to is easy to forward. A short summary on page one. Always.
Margins are where the page breathes. Cut them to fit more in and the page starts gasping.
Writers, a free one: the first line of a proposal should be about the client's ambition, not your services.
Documents in Recto are end-to-end encrypted. Private until you publish a link. We hold scrambled bytes, not your client's plans.
The hardest sentence in freelancing: "That's outside the scope. Here's what it would cost." Practise it. It gets easier.
Open Page: what's one habit that saved you hours this year? A template, a ritual, a rule, a sentence you now say early. Share it.
Every great presentation has a moment where the presenter stops talking and lets the slide work. Design for that moment.
The cover sells the document. The contents page sells the reading. Don't skip the second one.
An expiry date on a proposal isn't pressure. It's honesty. Your calendar and your prices both change.
A Recto link can carry a password and an expiry date, and you can unpublish it any time. Send with confidence. Take it back in one click.
Clients don't really pay for hours. They pay for the certainty that it'll be good. Price the certainty.
Ask a Kurdish designer about fonts and you'll hear the same story: a letter is missing, or it looks borrowed. Recto warns you when a font can't show a Kurdish letter, and offers one that can.
Clients judge your process by your paperwork. A messy invoice says messy studio. Fair or not.
Consistency is a decision you make once and benefit from forever. That's all a brand kit is.
What a client looks at when they open your proposal, in order:
The price. Then the timeline. Then the work samples. Then, if you're lucky, everything else.
So design for that order. A clear price, honest dates, strong samples.
And make "everything else" short enough to read in the lift.

Invoices live in Recto too. Your logo, a drawn signature or stamp, client details saved for next time, partial payments. The status moves from draft to sent, viewed, overdue and paid, so you always know where the money is.
You're allowed to say no to work that doesn't fit. Every wrong project takes the time of a right one.
Open Page: presenters, what's your rule for how much text goes on one slide? We'll start: if you have to read it aloud, it's too much.
A signature block at the end of a proposal changes how people read everything above it.
Numbered terms read like a promise. A paragraph of terms reads like a trap.
A payment schedule split into a deposit and milestones tells the client one thing: this person has done this before.
Search Unsplash photos, icons and illustrations from inside the Recto editor. Fewer tabs, more page.
Good creative teams argue about the work, never about which file is the latest. One brand kit, one set of templates, one version of the truth.
A bilingual document isn't two translations stapled together. It's one design that speaks twice.
A case study without a number is a story. Stories are lovely. Numbers get budgets approved.
Design the last page of the deck first. Once you know where it ends, every page before it has a direction.
"Just checking in" is the weakest follow-up there is. "I saw you spent time on the timeline. Any questions about the dates?" is the strongest.
Recto shows you who viewed your link, how long they spent on each page and how far they got. Write the follow-up with facts, not hope.
Every studio has a templates folder nobody trusts. Make one good template and the folder disappears.
Open Page: agencies and studios, how many pages is your ideal proposal? We've heard everything from 3 to 40. Defend your number.
The work wins the room. The document wins the budget meeting you weren't invited to.
Recto and verso: the right-hand page and the left. Every good document is a conversation between the two.
Your rate card should answer the question before the client asks it. If they have to email you for a price, half of them won't.
New in Recto Studio: folio.
Upload a finished identity: the logo, the guidelines, the mockups, the visual language.
One click turns it into an animated presentation page in that brand. It's built on your device and downloads as a single file you send to the client.
The brand handover, finally as good as the brand. justrecto.com
Designers undersell. Writers overexplain. Presenters overrun. Everybody overdelivers. Get paid for it.
To every designer setting Kurdish type with care: you're shaping how a language looks for the next generation. That's not a small job.
Make the document you'd want to receive. That's the whole brief.
